source.title: Do as I do (Safely): Mitigating Task-Specific Fine-tuning Risks in Large Language Models
source.authors: Francisco Eiras; Aleksandar Petrov; P. Torr; M. P. Kumar; Adel Bibi

record.file_problem: none; full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly measures harmful-completion rates after fine-tuning and refines the scope of benign fine-tuning risks: ordinary task-specific fine-tuning did not raise harmfulness, while some benign-looking adversarial formats did.
record.gate_note: Rows record harmful-query attack success rates after task-specific fine-tuning. The paper's comparisons with instruction-following fine-tuning from other studies are cited results, not rows. Task accuracy and toxicity-filter detection rates are not rows because they do not measure the claimed harmful-compliance behaviour. Safety-mixing mitigation results are also omitted because the claim versions do not ask whether this mitigation works.
record.test_reason: The study measures harmful-query ASR after benign task-specific fine-tuning of safety-trained models (LLaMA-2 7B Chat, LLaMA-3 8B, GPT-3.5). Ordinary task-specific formats left HarmI at 0%, while benign-looking adversarial formats (AOA, AutoIF, AutoIF+AOA) often raised it. This restates V2's scope.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that benign users are unlikely to accidentally obtain harmful models via task-specific fine-tuning, unlike the instruction-following setting. Malicious users can restructure task data into benign-looking formats (at most 0.61% flagged by moderation) that significantly raise harmfulness while keeping reasonable task accuracy. Their Paraphrase safety-mixing, which mimics the user's format, mitigates this more efficiently than Base or Longest mixing.
record.recipe_differences: The study tests fine-tuning on task-specific datasets such as PIQA, MMLU, and GSM8K, using Benign, AOA, AutoIF, and AutoIF + AOA prompt formats; it does not reproduce the original instruction-following fine-tuning recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Harmfulness varies by task dataset, prompting strategy, model, and evaluation set (HarmI versus HarmQ).
record.problems: The authors note that the adversarial strategies are demonstrative and may be detectable through structural analysis, and that the attacks are not controllable or guaranteed stable. The GPT-3.5 results cover only PIQA and are less reproducible because the API model's internal process is unavailable. Safety judgments use an automated HarmBench judge; a human check covered 120 samples and reported 92.5% agreement.
record.rows_left_out: To stay within the 60-row cap, omitted HarmQ results for LLaMA-2 AutoIF and AutoIF + AOA conditions in Appendix E, Table 7, and the separate safety-mixing results in Appendix E, Table 10. Also omitted the number-of-epochs figure in Appendix G, which is described qualitatively rather than with tabulated values.

untested.parts: Ordinary instruction-following benign data (Alpaca, Dolly) is only cited from Qi et al., not re-run.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks. The Anti-AOA system prompt is a mitigation, not a bypass test.
No causal test of why alignment is shallow.
No deepening training. Safety-data mixing is not token-depth training.

missing.what: PIQA dataset mixing 1/3 AOA, 1/3 AutoIF, 1/3 AutoIF+AOA, fine-tuned without safety mixing: HarmI 7.50%, HarmQ 54.00% (baselines 0% / 19%), LLaMA-2 7B

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. AOA comes from Qi et al.'s identity-shifting attack, which fits V2's 'carefully chosen benign data'; AutoIF is closer to ordinary instruction-style conversion. The authors claim no BoolQ strategy gave 'a marked increase', yet Table 7 reports BoolQ(B) AutoIF+AOA HarmQ at 56% vs 19%, so the text overstates BoolQ's safety. Fine-tuning uses LoRA 8-bit for 1 epoch, and AutoIF variants train on only 1% of each dataset. There is a single run, no uncertainty, and a HarmBench judge with 92.5% agreement on 120 human-checked samples. The epoch ablation (Fig. 9) reports AutoIF harmfulness falling with more epochs, qualitatively.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not fine-tune on harmful examples.
It studies task-specific datasets and benign-looking adversarial prompt formats, not ordinary instruction-following fine-tuning as in the claim's original setting.
No per-token KL measurement or response-position analysis.
No compliant-opening prefill, adversarial suffix, or decoding-change test. The Anti-AOA system prompt is a prompt-based mitigation, not a test of getting past a compliant opening.
No parameter localization, weight ablation, or rank analysis.
No test of whether the data or training objective causes first-token shallowness.
No training designed to spread safety beyond initial response tokens.

relationships.condition: Ordinary (Benign-template) task-specific fine-tuning, LLaMA-2 7B on 8 datasets, LLaMA-3 8B and GPT-3.5 on PIQA
relationships.reason: HarmI stays at 0% (0.19% for GPT-3.5). HarmQ is at or below baseline (14–18% vs 19%; 0% vs 17% for LLaMA-3) (r01,r05,r09,r13,r17,r21,r25,r29,r33,r37,r41-r48,r57).
relationships.display_finding: HarmI stayed at 0% (0.19% for GPT-3.5), and HarmQ stayed at or below baseline: 14–18% versus 19%, and 0% versus 17% for LLaMA-3.

relationships.condition: Benign-looking adversarial formats (AOA, AutoIF, AutoIF+AOA) where ASR rises
relationships.reason: HarmI rises from 0% to 5–84% for LLaMA-2 and to 64–65% for LLaMA-3 (AutoIF variants). GPT-3.5 reaches 28–56%. HarmQ rises to 25–74% (r03,r04,r06-r08,r10,r12,r15,r16,r19,r20,r22,r23,r26-r28,r30-r32,r35,r36,r38-r40,r51,r54-r56,r59,r60).
relationships.display_finding: HarmI ASR rose from 0% to 5–84% for LLaMA-2 and to 64–65% for LLaMA-3 with AutoIF variants, and reached 28–56% for GPT-3.5; HarmQ ASR rose to 25–74%.

relationships.condition: Adversarial formats on some datasets and models (notably AOA on BoolQ, HellaSwag, MMLU, and on LLaMA-3 PIQA)
relationships.reason: The effect is strongly dataset- and format-dependent. HarmI rises only 0.2–4%, and HarmQ falls below or matches baseline in several AOA settings (r02,r11,r14,r18,r24,r34,r49,r50,r52,r53,r58).
relationships.display_finding: The effect depended strongly on dataset and format: HarmI rose only 0.2–4%, and HarmQ fell below or matched baseline in several AOA settings.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Ordinary Benign task-specific fine-tuning across the reported LLaMA-2 datasets and LLaMA-3 PIQA
reader_labels.reason: HarmI ASR remained at 0.00% for the listed LLaMA-2 and LLaMA-3 Benign conditions, and HarmQ ASR was below the original-model baseline in all included Benign rows (r01, r05, r09, r13, r17, r21, r25, r29, r33, r41-r48, r57).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Benign-looking adversarial task-specific formats, in settings where HarmI or HarmQ ASR rises
reader_labels.reason: AOA, AutoIF, or AutoIF + AOA produced higher harmful-response rates in several datasets and models, including high rates on PIQA and HellaSwag; results vary across formats and settings (r02-r04, r06-r08, r10-r12, r14-r16, r18-r20, r22-r24, r26-r28, r30-r32, r34-r40, r51, r54-r56, r59-r60).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Adversarial task-specific formats where the increase was small, absent, or varied by model, dataset, or evaluation set
reader_labels.reason: Some increases were small, and several AOA conditions did not increase HarmQ ASR or were below baseline; results therefore do not support an unconditional effect across formats and settings (r02, r11, r14, r18, r24, r34, r49-r50, r52-r53, r58).
